name: Hip and knee joint replacements can last longer

content.title: Hip and knee joint replacements can last longer
content.summary: Improvement in materials and recent advances in surgical techniques means that most active patients requiring hip and knee implants will be able to use their joint replacements for as long as 15 to 20 years.

media.alt: Hip and knee joint replacements can last longer

content.text: Improvement in materials and recent advances in surgical techniques means that most active patients requiring hip and knee implants will be able to use their joint replacements for as long as 15 to 20 years, according to doctors at Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH) speaking on the occasion of Bone and Joint Day to raise awareness about common bone and joint problems.

Speaking about hip and knee replacement surgeries, Dr Shahryar Noordin, Consultant Orthopaedic Surgeon, AKUH, pointed out that newer designs allow patients much more flexibility. Modern knee replacements allow people greater knee bending movement, which is especially useful for people who do activities that involve kneeling. Similar long-term results are seen with total hip replacement surgeries. He described that currently, about one million total hip and total knee replacement surgeries are performed worldwide each year and by the year 2030, it is projected that these numbers will increase three- to four-fold.

Dr Muhammad Wajid, Consultant Orthopaedic Surgeon, AKUH, speaking about shoulder pain, said that there are usually two groups of people suffering from shoulder problems: the middle aged or elderly, and those involved in sports. In many cases, shoulder pain is due to wear and tear of muscles, which reduces a person's ability to perform regular activities, such as sleeping on the affected side or dressing themselves. People with existing shoulder injuries, such as a dislocation, may be prone to repeated complications with even minor injuries. Most of these conditions can be treated with care and proper monitoring. In severe cases, a patient may require keyhole surgery, where the whole procedure is carried out through two or three small holes made in the bone. "Performed as day-care surgery - where most patient return home on the same day - there is less pain, better healing of the wound and early movements with improved outcomes," said Dr Wajid.

Since a growing number of people suffer from diabetes, Dr Tashfeen Ahmad, Consultant Orthopaedic Surgeon, AKUH, explained that improvements in research have provided a better understanding of the effects of diabetes on different parts of the body, and specifically, on the foot. "Foot ulcers and bone or joint issues identified in the early stages stand a good chance of being treated successfully," said Dr Ahmad. He added that a diabetic patient requires a team approach that involves physicians, surgeons, nurses and podiatrists.

Exercise can prevent age-related changes to muscles, bones and joints, and in some cases, can reverse these changes also. "Exercise helps keep joints flexible, strengthens the muscles around joints and makes bones stronger," said Asim Mahmood, Charge Physiotherapist, AKUH. For the elderly, muscle-strengthening activities, balance and coordination exercises can increase muscle mass and can help reduce the risk of falls. Physical activity in later life may delay the progression of osteoporosis, as it slows down the rate at which bone mineral density is reduced. Aerobics, walking and weight training exercises are the best way to maintain bone mass and prevent arthritic changes in the joints. He added that stretching can also help maintain joint flexibility. "It's never too late to start living an active lifestyle at any age," said Mahmood.
